extracted.intended_audience: philosophers of mathematics, mathematical logicians, computer scientists in formal verification, and mathematics educators
extracted.subtask_description: Clarifying what it is to 'understand' a mathematical proof by analyzing it as possession of particular abilities and by mapping those abilities to practice, pedagogy, and formal verification. Focuses on characterizing abilities that justify ascriptions of understanding and illustrating them with case studies in formal methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understanding as possession of abilities
rubrics_metrics.description: Ascriptions of understanding are best analyzed in terms of an agent's possession of certain abilities or capacities (e.g., to do, to discover, to apply), rather than as mere mental states or only as possession of a proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Philosophically, this reframes 'understanding X' as 'having relevant abilities regarding X'. This avoids mystical appeals to 'grasping' and focuses on specifying the network of abilities appropriate to particular contexts; useful for pedagogy and for designing systems that model mathematical competence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ability to determine correctness and fill in details on demand
rubrics_metrics.description: The ability to respond to challenges about the correctness of a proof by filling in missing details and justifying inferences when a skeptic asks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the baseline epistemic ability: supplying missing inferences, giving formal justifications, and defending steps under scrutiny. It aligns with the traditional logical standard that a proof should be checkable, but emphasizes interactive competence (responding to requests for detail).

rubrics_metrics.name: Ability to give a high-level outline or overview
rubrics_metrics.description: The ability to present a proof at a higher level of abstraction, giving an overview that captures the main ideas and structure rather than only line-by-line derivations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This captures the explanatory aspect of understanding: being able to summarize the architecture of an argument so others can see the flow and main mechanisms without reconstructing every inference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ability to recast a proof in different terms
rubrics_metrics.description: The ability to cast the proof in different terminology or formalisms, e.g., eliminating or adding abstract terminology or translating between frameworks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Useful for communicating with different audiences, for relating the argument to other areas, and for clarifying which aspects are conceptual versus notational/terminological.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ability to identify key or novel points versus straightforward steps
rubrics_metrics.description: The ability to indicate which steps of the argument are the 'key' or novel contributions and to separate them from those that are routine or straightforward.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This helps judge the intellectual contribution of a proof, explains why later proofs can still be valuable (they may highlight different key ideas), and guides exposition by focusing attention on the nontrivial moves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ability to motivate the proof (explain why steps are natural)
rubrics_metrics.description: The ability to 'motivate' the proof by explaining why certain steps are natural or to be expected, i.e., why the argument proceeds as it does rather than by 'caprice'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes explaining why particular definitions, constructions, or intermediate claims were chosen and how they lead toward the end; ties into the logic of discovery and pedagogical exposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ability to provide natural examples illustrating phenomena
rubrics_metrics.description: The ability to give natural examples that exhibit the phenomena or constructions that occur in the proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples ground abstract arguments, clarify hypotheses, and make the content accessible; providing examples is part of demonstrating understanding and teaching.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ability to indicate where hypotheses are used and give counterexamples
rubrics_metrics.description: The ability to point out where particular hypotheses of a theorem are needed and, where appropriate, to give counterexamples showing failure if hypotheses are omitted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This ability explains the role and necessity of assumptions, illuminates the theorem's limits, and is valuable both philosophically and pedagogically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ability to view the proof as a generalization or adaptation of known proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: The ability to recognize and present the proof as a parallel development, e.g., as a generalization, adaptation, or straightforward modification of a familiar proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relating a proof to known patterns aids comprehension, suggests transfer to new problems, and helps place the result within the mathematical landscape.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ability to propose generalizations and interesting weakenings
rubrics_metrics.description: The ability to offer generalizations of the theorem or to suggest interesting weakenings of the conclusion that correspond to weakening hypotheses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This reflects a forward-looking aspect of understanding: using the method to generate new results and to see how the argument scales or fails under changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ability to compute or explicitly construct objects guaranteed by the theorem
rubrics_metrics.description: The ability to calculate particular quantities or to provide explicit descriptions/constructions of objects whose existence the theorem asserts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contributes to concrete understanding and applicability; an existence proof accompanied by a constructive description exhibits stronger practical understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ability to represent the argument diagrammatically
rubrics_metrics.description: The ability to provide a diagram representing some of the data in the proof or to relate the proof to a particular diagram.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Diagrams can make structure and intuition visible, aiding both discovery and exposition; visualization is a legitimate component of mathematical understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ability to supply missing inferences, draw analogies, and discover related theorems
rubrics_metrics.description: The ability to supply missing inferences in a sketchy argument, to draw appropriate analogies, and to discover or predict related theorems by seeing general methods in the structure of the argument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are the cognitive maneuvers associated with 'Aha!' moments: recognizing patterns that allow anticipation of steps or transfer of methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understanding includes seeing how a proof could have been discovered
rubrics_metrics.description: Part of understanding is seeing how the proof could have been discovered, i.e., having insight into the discovery process or the route by which the argument would naturally be found.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Links the epistemology of justification with the 'logic of discovery'; being able to reconstruct plausible discovery paths is central to explanatory understanding and to teaching heuristics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understanding as discernment/selection in discovery (Poincaré)
rubrics_metrics.description: Discovery and thus understanding consist in discriminating useful combinations from the vast space of possibilities — 'discernment, selection' of the small minority of fruitful paths.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasizes heuristic judgment and taste in mathematics; appreciating why certain definitions/moves are chosen is part of understanding and cannot be reduced to merely checking correctness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ascriptions of understanding are justified by behavior across uses (Wittgensteinian view)
rubrics_metrics.description: From a Wittgensteinian perspective, the meaning of mathematical expressions and ascriptions of understanding are determined by use in practice; we should clarify the circumstances (array of uses) under which we are willing to ascribe understanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Philosophical therapy: instead of positing hidden mental states, explicate the observable linguistic/behavioral criteria (contexts, performances, capacities) that justify saying someone 'understands' a concept or proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understanding must be characterized with scope restrictions to avoid extraneous factors
rubrics_metrics.description: A useful theory of mathematical understanding should bracket irrelevant beliefs, desires, and pathological circumstances (e.g., incapacity to perform despite competence), focusing on mathematical intentions and contexts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This responds to criticisms of dispositional accounts: specify ceteris paribus conditions and limit scope to mathematical behavior so the account remains informative and applicable to pedagogy and formal modeling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theory of understanding should be action-guiding (useful for pedagogy and software)
rubrics_metrics.description: A satisfactory account of mathematical understanding should not only identify behaviors but also offer guidance for fostering those abilities (in teaching) and implementing them (in automated reasoning/formal verification).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pragmatic desideratum: the theory should inform expository practice, curriculum design, and the design of computational systems that aim to exhibit or support mathematical understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understanding goes beyond correctness: proofs can increase understanding without changing truth-value
rubrics_metrics.description: Later proofs of a theorem, even after its truth is established, can be important because they augment understanding (offer new perspectives, methods, or explanations) rather than changing the fact of correctness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluations of proofs should include their explanatory power, novelty of approach, and contribution to the network of abilities and concepts, not just whether they establish the theorem.
